items.title: Detect direct prompt injection against LLM-backed features
items.objective: Determine whether a directly submitted prompt can override the documented instruction boundaries of an LLM-backed web feature and redirect its tools, retrieval, or data access.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its connected tools
An isolated test account, synthetic data, and a harmless canary tool or read target
Documentation of the feature's intended instruction boundaries and tool scopes
steps: Map every direct prompt input and the tools, functions, and data sources the model can call on behalf of the caller
Send ordinary baseline prompts and record which tools and data the model legitimately reaches
Send crafted prompts that request one out-of-scope tool call or protected read at a time, targeting the harmless canary only
Observe whether the request is refused, described, or actually executed
Correlate any executed action with tool logs and the isolated canary account before drawing conclusions

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One instruction boundary, connected tool, or data scope at a time
items.secure_behavior: The feature treats every prompt as untrusted input, re-validates tool calls against the caller's authorization, and never lets model output reach sensitive sinks unchecked.
items.vulnerable_behavior: a crafted prompt causes a tool call, retrieval, or state change outside the caller's authorization
items.validation: Correlate the prompt with an observed tool call, log entry, or state change under the isolated canary account; a persuasive model reply without a confirmed action is not a finding.
false_positives: the model may describe an action in text without executing it
demo or sandboxed integrations may simulate tool calls instead of performing them
items.impact: Confirmed prompt injection can perform unauthorized actions through connected tools, read data the model can reach, or inject content that reaches other users.
evidence: Authorized scope covering the LLM feature and connected tools
Exact prompt, channel, and observed tool call or state change
Canary-account request/response pairs and server-side tool logs

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Use an isolated canary tool and synthetic data only. Never test prompt injection through real user content, live customer data, or destructive tool calls; stop if model behavior could affect other users.
items.remediation: Treat all prompt content as untrusted; validate model-chosen tool calls against caller authorization, minimize tool scopes, require confirmation for consequential actions, and never let the model read data the caller cannot read.
do_not_report: Do not report a model reply that merely describes or invents an action as injection; demonstrate an executed tool call, retrieval, or state change under the isolated canary account before reporting.

items.title: Detect indirect prompt injection through retrieved content
items.objective: Determine whether instructions hidden inside documents, web pages, messages, or other content the model retrieves can steer an LLM-backed feature into unauthorized behavior for the requesting user.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its retrieval sources
An isolated test account and a document or message the tester controls end to end
A harmless canary action that proves model steering without real impact
steps: Identify which retrieved sources (uploaded files, emails, web pages, tickets) feed the model without user review
Place a benign instruction inside a tester-controlled document and request the feature summarizes or acts on it
Observe whether the embedded instruction changes model behavior, tool calls, or output for the requesting user
Repeat with one instruction and one channel at a time, including markup or fake-response framing only as comparison cases
Confirm any effect against the caller's real authorization with the canary action

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One indirect input channel, embedded instruction, or connected tool at a time
items.secure_behavior: Retrieved content is marked as untrusted data, instructions from retrieved sources are neutralized or ignored, and all resulting actions stay within the caller's authorization.
items.vulnerable_behavior: an instruction embedded in retrieved content reliably changes model behavior or triggers an action for the requesting user
items.validation: Correlate the embedded instruction with an observed behavior change or tool action under the canary account; a changed wording without security effect is not a finding.
false_positives: the model may summarize the embedded instruction without following it
retrieval quality filters can drop injected content before the model sees it
items.impact: Confirmed indirect injection can turn any user-reachable content into an instruction channel, enabling data exposure, unauthorized tool calls, or persistent manipulation for later users.
evidence: Authorized scope and retrieval-source inventory
The tester-controlled document and its embedded instruction
Observed model output, tool call, or state change under the canary account

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Deliver injected instructions only through content you own end to end and only to your isolated test account. Never seed shared corpora, customer documents, or production indexes; stop if other users could encounter the content.
items.remediation: Separate untrusted retrieved content from instructions at the model boundary, neutralize instruction-like text in retrieved data, and authorize every resulting action against the caller rather than the model's interpretation.
do_not_report: Do not report a summarization that echoes an embedded instruction as injection; demonstrate a security-relevant behavior change or action traceable to the injected content.

items.title: Prevent disclosure of system prompts and internal instructions
items.objective: Determine whether an LLM-backed feature reveals its system prompt, retrieval rules, or hidden instructions that disclose business logic, data sources, or bypass guidance.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature
An isolated test account with the same privilege tier as the intended attacker
steps: Send ordinary prompts and record what configuration details the feature volunteers
Ask the model to restate its instructions, rules, or earlier messages using several phrasings
Compare disclosures against what the product documentation already publishes
Record whether non-public instructions, tool schemas, or data-source details appear in responses
Repeat across channels (chat, API, generated summaries) before concluding

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One disclosure target (instructions, tool schema, retrieval rules) and one channel at a time
items.secure_behavior: The feature discloses only what the product publishes; hidden instructions, internal tool schemas, and retrieval rules stay non-public.
items.vulnerable_behavior: responses reveal non-public system instructions, tool definitions, data-source details, or guardrail descriptions that materially assist further attacks
items.validation: Require non-public content in the response that matches internal configuration and assists an attack step; publicly documented product text is not a finding.
false_positives: the model may restate public product documentation
guardrail descriptions can be generic and low value without revealing internal structure
items.impact: Disclosed instructions and tool schemas give attackers a map of connected tools, validation rules, and bypass paths, compounding other LLM weaknesses.
evidence: Exact prompts and responses
Comparison against published product documentation
Assessment of which disclosure assists a subsequent attack step

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Probe only with your isolated test account and never extract credentials, keys, or real user data as part of the test; record only redacted responses.
items.remediation: Design prompts so hidden instructions cannot be reproduced, avoid embedding secrets or schemas in system prompts, and filter or refuse instruction-recitation requests at the model boundary.
do_not_report: Do not report restatements of public product documentation as a finding; require non-public instructions, tool schemas, or data-source details that materially assist further attacks.

items.title: Enforce authorization on retrieved and grounded content
items.objective: Determine whether retrieval-augmented features return documents or records the caller is not authorized to read, regardless of which prompt triggered the retrieval.
prerequisites: Written authorization and two isolated test accounts with different data access
A synthetic restricted document owned by one account and not the other
steps: Identify the knowledge base, vector index, or document store backing retrieval answers
Submit questions from the unrestricted account that should only be answerable using the restricted account's document
Probe with paraphrases and multi-document questions to test retrieval versus answer-level filtering
Repeat from the restricted account to confirm the document is retrievable when authorized
Record which prompts returned restricted content to the unauthorized caller

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One restricted document, one requesting account, and one retrieval path at a time
items.secure_behavior: Every retrieved chunk is authorization-checked against the requesting caller before the model can read or cite it.
items.vulnerable_behavior: an unauthorized caller receives content from, or answers derived from, a document they cannot read
items.validation: Require the response to contain content only derivable from the restricted document and attributable to retrieval, not general knowledge; confirm the caller lacks direct access to the document.
false_positives: the model may answer from general knowledge that overlaps the document
retrieval may return only public metadata while the answer stays harmless
items.impact: Unauthorized retrieval turns the model into an oracle for documents the caller cannot open, leaking customer data, secrets, or tenant-restricted records at query speed.
evidence: Account and permission evidence for both test identities
Prompts and responses containing restricted content
Retrieval logs or index identifiers showing the source document

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026

items.safety: Use only synthetic documents and isolated test accounts; never query the system with real customer data or attempt to retrieve live restricted records.
items.remediation: Apply the caller's access controls to retrieval results before grounding, index per-document ACLs, and audit answers for content only derivable from the caller's authorized set.
items.retest_guidance: After remediation, retest with a new restricted synthetic document across paraphrased and multi-document prompts from both accounts, and confirm retrieval logs show the ACL was applied before the model saw the content.

items.title: Detect retrieval corpus poisoning that steers model behavior
items.objective: Determine whether attacker-influenced content in the retrieval corpus, such as uploaded documents or public pages, can change model answers or actions for other users.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the retrieval corpus and its ingestion pipeline
A synthetic poisoned document the tester controls from creation to indexing
steps: Identify which user-influenced content enters the corpus and when it is indexed
Create a synthetic document containing a harmless steering instruction and unique marker
Trigger ingestion through the normal user workflow and wait for the documented indexing window
Query the feature from a second account and observe whether the marker or instruction changes answers
Remove the document and confirm the effect disappears before ending the test

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One poisoned document, one instruction, and one query pattern at a time
items.secure_behavior: Corpus content is treated as untrusted data, ingestion requires authorization, and answers derive from validated sources without instruction-following from indexed text.
items.vulnerable_behavior: a poisoned document reliably changes answers, citations, or tool behavior for other users
items.validation: Require the marker to appear in responses to a second account, attributable to the poisoned document, and reproducible after re-indexing; confirm removal ends the effect.
false_positives: search or retrieval ranking can surface the document without changing answers
similar legitimate content may coincidentally produce overlapping answers
items.impact: Corpus poisoning provides persistent, cross-user steering: false answers, phishing content, or instruction injection that survives individual prompt defenses.
evidence: The poisoned document and ingestion evidence
Queries and responses from a second account showing the marker
Timeline showing effect removal after document deletion

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026

items.safety: Only inject synthetic documents you own and can remove; never poison shared corpora or production indexes, and verify removal restores baseline behavior before finishing.
items.remediation: Validate and neutralize instruction-like content at ingestion, authorize corpus writes, and treat indexed content as untrusted data at answer time.
do_not_report: Do not report a poisoned document that merely surfaces in citations without changing answers or behavior; require a reproducible steering effect on other users.

items.title: Neutralize injected payloads in LLM-generated tool arguments
items.objective: Determine whether arguments the model produces for tools such as SQL queries, shell helpers, or path selectors can carry interpreter payloads that the tool executes.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its connected tools
An isolated test account and a harmless canary endpoint or query target
Documentation of which tools accept model-generated arguments
steps: Map every tool the model can call and the interpreter each argument feeds
Request operations that legitimately exercise each tool with a baseline argument
Embed one inert payload candidate (SQL predicate, path segment, or command separator) in the request and observe the generated argument
Use paired controls to distinguish model-generation defects from normal argument handling
Confirm any execution against the harmless canary before concluding

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One tool, one argument position, and one payload family at a time
items.secure_behavior: Model-generated arguments are parameterized, allowlisted, and validated exactly like caller-supplied input before any interpreter executes them.
items.vulnerable_behavior: a payload survives model generation and the tool executes it in a way caller-supplied input would not be allowed to reach
items.validation: Require a confirmed interpreter effect at the harmless canary, such as a paired boolean difference or a marker row, not just a suspicious generated argument.
false_positives: the model may reproduce the payload as literal text without execution
downstream validators can reject the payload even when the model generated it
items.impact: Confirmation means prompt injection becomes arbitrary interpreter access through the tool, potentially reading or modifying data the caller cannot reach directly.
evidence: Tool inventory and the exact prompt used
The generated argument and the canary response pair
Logs showing which component executed the argument

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Test only inert payload candidates against an isolated canary target; never execute destructive commands or query production data through model-generated arguments.
items.remediation: Treat model output as untrusted input: parameterize all interpreter calls, allowlist tool schemas, and validate every generated argument at the tool boundary.
items.retest_guidance: After remediation, retest each tool with the original payload family and one adjacent variant, and confirm the tool rejects the argument before the interpreter receives it.

items.title: Constrain LLM tool agency to the caller's authority
items.objective: Determine whether an LLM-backed feature can invoke privileged or consequential tools without explicit user confirmation, reauthentication, or a per-call authorization check.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its tools
Test accounts at two privilege levels with isolated canary actions
steps: Inventory every tool the model can invoke and the authority each requires
From the low-privilege account, prompt for a canary action that only the high-privilege role may perform
Test whether the feature asks for confirmation, reauthenticates, or silently forwards the call
Repeat for consequential categories such as sends, purchases, exports, and settings changes
Confirm any executed action against tool logs and the isolated canary

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One tool, one privilege boundary, and one confirmation control at a time
items.secure_behavior: Every consequential tool call requires the caller's authorization, user confirmation for irreversible actions, and step-up where policy requires it.
items.vulnerable_behavior: a low-privilege caller triggers a privileged tool action without confirmation, reauthentication, or a failed authorization check
items.validation: Require an executed privileged action observable in logs or canary state, attributable to the low-privilege account; a suggested action that the user declined is not a finding.
false_positives: the feature may present the action for approval without executing it
administrative tools can be available only to elevated sessions the tester cannot reach
items.impact: Excessive agency lets any prompt-wielding user perform privileged actions through the model, bypassing authorization and audit controls that protect the same actions in the normal UI.
evidence: Role and permission evidence for both test accounts
Prompts, approval prompts, and the executed action
Tool logs and canary state changes

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Trigger only canary actions on test-owned objects; never send real notifications, purchases, or exports, and stop if an action could affect production users.
items.remediation: Bind each tool to the caller's authorization at invocation time, require confirmation for consequential actions, and keep model-suggested actions out of privileged paths.
items.retest_guidance: After remediation, retest the same privilege boundary with a paraphrased prompt and an adjacent tool in the same category, and confirm authorization and confirmation both hold.

items.title: Validate LLM output before rendering and downstream parsing
items.objective: Determine whether model-generated output reaches HTML, Markdown, or structured parsers without the same validation applied to user input, enabling stored cross-site scripting or parser injection for other users.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its output consumers
An isolated test account and a second account to observe stored effects
steps: Identify every sink that consumes model output: chat renderers, summaries, emails, exports, and downstream parsers
Submit prompts that ask the model to reproduce a harmless marker payload for one sink at a time
Observe whether the output is encoded, sanitized, or executed at the sink
Use paired prompts and direct user-input controls to compare the pipeline for model output versus ordinary input
Confirm execution only at a harmless local canary or with the second isolated account

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One output sink, one payload family, and one consumer at a time
items.secure_behavior: Model output is treated as untrusted data: encoded for its rendering context and validated before any parser consumes it.
items.vulnerable_behavior: model-generated content executes at a browser or parser sink that direct user input is prevented from reaching
items.validation: Require an observed execution or parse-level effect at the canary, attributable to model output; a raw payload in the response body that nothing executes is not a finding.
false_positives: the renderer may sanitize model output even when direct input is unsanitized
the payload may be reproduced in a non-executing context such as code formatting
items.impact: Confirmed output handling turns any prompt-wielding user into a stored injection source for every consumer of model text, including privileged reviewers.
evidence: The prompt, the model output, and the sink context
Canary execution evidence or the second account's observed effect
Comparison against the same payload submitted as direct user input

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Execute payloads only at a harmless local canary or inside your isolated second account; never inject into shared review queues or production content.
items.remediation: Route model output through the same context-aware encoding and sanitization as user input, and validate it at every parser boundary before use.
items.retest_guidance: After remediation, retest the original sink and one adjacent consumer (chat, export, notification) with the same payload family, and confirm encoding or sanitization before execution.

items.title: Prevent cross-user and cross-tenant LLM context leakage
items.objective: Determine whether shared model memory, conversation reuse, caching, or vector-store indexing exposes one user's or tenant's data in another user's responses.
prerequisites: Written authorization and isolated test accounts in two tenants or ownership contexts
Synthetic marker data visible to only one of the accounts
steps: Map where conversation state, memory, and index data persist between requests and accounts
Seed a unique synthetic marker through one account's normal feature use
Query the feature from the second account with prompts likely to surface prior context
Test session reuse, account switching, tenant switching, and shared caches as separate conditions
Record any response containing the first account's marker and attribute the leak path

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One persistence boundary (memory, cache, index) and one account pair at a time
items.secure_behavior: Conversation state, memory, and retrieval are partitioned per account and tenant, and responses never cite data from outside the caller's context.
items.vulnerable_behavior: one account's synthetic marker appears in another account's responses or retrievals
items.validation: Require the unique marker to appear in the second account's response and attribute it to the shared store; coincidental wording is not a finding.
false_positives: generic phrasing can resemble the marker without data leakage
a shared public knowledge source can legitimately contain the same information
items.impact: Cross-context leakage exposes customer data, secrets, and tenant-confidential content across the boundary the application exists to enforce.
evidence: Account and tenant setup evidence
The synthetic marker and the leaking prompt/response pair
Logs or store identifiers showing the shared persistence path

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026

items.safety: Use only synthetic markers in isolated test accounts; never attempt to surface real customer or tenant data during testing.
items.remediation: Partition model state, memory, and retrieval indexes by account and tenant, purge context on identity changes, and exclude cross-tenant sources from grounding.

items.title: Constrain URL-fetching tools behind LLM features
items.objective: Determine whether prompts can steer a model-connected URL tool toward internal, metadata, or otherwise prohibited destinations that the application would normally reject.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its URL tool
A controlled callback destination under the tester's control
Documentation of the tool's intended destination policy
steps: Map the URL tool's reachable protocols, hosts, and ports through normal feature use
Request a fetch of the controlled callback and record the request fingerprint
Attempt one prohibited destination class at a time using the same phrasing patterns as the baseline
Distinguish tool-level requests from browser-side requests made by the tester's own client
Repeat with redirects or alternate representations only where the owner has approved the probe

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One destination class, one redirect or representation condition, and one tool at a time
items.secure_behavior: URL tools enforce the same allowlists, resolution checks, and egress policy as other fetchers, and prompts cannot widen the destination set.
items.vulnerable_behavior: the model tool requests a destination outside the approved policy and the request originates server-side
items.validation: Require a server-side request observed at the controlled destination with a unique marker and matching timing; client-side requests from the tester's browser are excluded.
false_positives: the tester's own browser may issue requests that look like the tool
public destination policies can legitimately include the probed host
items.impact: A confirmed fetch reaches internal services, cloud metadata, or private hosts through a path ordinary SSRF controls do not inspect.
evidence: The callback log with the unique marker and source address
The exact prompt and tool invocation
Evidence the request came from the tool, not the browser

references.title: Web LLM attacks
OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

items.safety: Probe only your controlled callback and owner-approved destinations; never target metadata endpoints, internal services, or third parties without explicit authorization.
items.remediation: Apply the application's SSRF allowlists and egress policy to model-invoked URL tools, validate resolved addresses, and revalidate redirects at connection time.
items.retest_guidance: After remediation, retest with a redirect from the allowed destination to a prohibited one and confirm the tool revalidates before connecting.

items.title: Bound LLM generation and tool-loop resource use
items.objective: Determine whether an unauthenticated or low-privilege caller can trigger unbounded generation, repeated tool invocations, or expensive retrieval that creates disproportionate cost or service degradation.
prerequisites: Written authorization covering the LLM feature and its billing model
An isolated test account and the documented usage limits
steps: Identify the per-call and per-principal limits on generation length, tool calls, and retrieval depth
Submit requests that request maximum-length output, repeated tool loops, and deep retrieval chains
Measure tokens, tool invocations, and wall time against the documented limits
Test whether parallel or repeated requests accumulate beyond per-principal budgets
Stop at the documented ceiling and record what the system enforces versus allows

examples.note: Use an isolated canary action (for example a marker write to a test-owned record) instead of real tool calls, user data, or production state.

items.manipulate: One resource dimension (output length, tool loops, retrieval depth) at a time
items.secure_behavior: Generation, tool-call counts, and retrieval are bounded per principal and per call, with cost accounting that cannot be exceeded through phrasing alone.
items.vulnerable_behavior: requests beyond documented budgets succeed, or repeated calls accumulate cost far beyond the per-principal allowance
items.validation: Require measured consumption beyond the documented limit with attributable cost or degradation; slow responses within policy are not a finding.
false_positives: longer outputs within the published limit are intended behavior
provider-side throttling can mask per-application budget gaps on small samples
items.impact: Unbounded use converts the feature into a cost or availability primitive for any caller, and can degrade shared capacity for other tenants.
evidence: The documented limits and the measured consumption
Request/response pairs and tool-call counts
Cost or degradation evidence attributable to the test account

references.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026

items.safety: Stay within documented limits and stop before any measurable degradation; never run sustained loops against shared production capacity.
items.remediation: Enforce per-principal and per-call budgets on tokens, tool invocations, and retrieval, and reject requests that cannot be accounted against the caller.
do_not_report: Do not report responses within published limits as abuse; measure consumption beyond the documented budget or demonstrate a path to disproportionate cost before reporting.
